raw_response:
I farm only 1.1 mu, so I cannot afford to take big risks. What I do is mostly what has worked on my land and what people around me are doing. For wheat, I will still put a bit more attention on fertilizer and water, because if wheat is weak in spring, yield falls quickly and I cannot make that back later. The extension people say one rate, but on my field I usually go a little steady rather than too low. I will sow wheat in early October, use a local improved variety that people nearby trust, put most of the fertilizer as base, then add some urea at jointing if the leaves are not dark enough. Since I have well water, I plan for about three irrigations for wheat, but if spring rain is decent, I may save one to reduce pumping cost.

For maize, the main thing is speed after wheat harvest. The gap is short, and with some family members working off-farm, I do not want to waste days on heavy tillage. So after harvesting wheat, I will quickly clear the field, do light rotary tillage or direct seeding if I can arrange it, and plant hybrid maize right away in mid-June. Maize usually gets less water than wheat here unless it turns dry at tasseling. I will still use fertilizer, but not too much, because cash is tight and maize on this small plot mainly needs to be reliable, not fancy. I will watch weeds and corn borer, spray if I see a problem, and keep the plan close to what has worked in recent years.
